posts.cooked:
Started with one supplier because it was simpler. One relationship, one lead time, one quality standard to manage. Made sense at the beginning.

But watching what happened to sellers dependent on a single source when tariffs hit this year made us rethink everything. One delayed shipment now means stock hitting zero across every channel simultaneously.

Curious how others think about this.

Is there a volume or revenue threshold where diversifying becomes non-negotiable? Or is it more about the category some products just too risky to single-source regardless of size?

And for those who’ve diversified how do you manage quality consistency across multiple suppliers without it becoming a full-time job?

Early on, I do not diversify just because orders are growing. I diversify when one supplier starts becoming one point of failure.

A few triggers for me:

  • the order size is now painful if one shipment slips
  • lead times start drifting
  • paperwork or payment details stop being consistent
  • there is no realistic backup for the same spec

I still like having one main supplier at the start, but I want a second option mapped before the order gets big enough to hurt. Quality across two suppliers only works if your specs and checkpoints are tighter than the relationship.

Hi @Techspawn2 .
Hope you are having a good day.
Find a backup supplier now, before you need one.
If losing you currently supplies empty your shelves for more than 30 days, you are already very exposed.
Give the backup of 30% of your orders to keep the relationship real, and pick one in a different country; traffic doesn’t hit both at once.

Agree on building the backup before it is urgent. I would still test the backup with the same spec sheet and a small real order first. Otherwise the backup can look fine on paper but fail at the first handoff.

On the second half of your question, keeping quality consistent across several suppliers, what works best is making the spec yours, not theirs:

  • Keep a signed “golden sample” and give each supplier an identical copy.
  • Write a one-page spec sheet: materials, colours, dimensions, packaging, labels, accessories in the box. Ask both factories to quote against that sheet, not their own catalogue item.
  • Ask for test reports in each supplier’s own name for that exact model; a report from supplier A doesn’t cover supplier B.
  • Use the same pre-shipment inspection checklist for both, and mark batch codes on the cartons so you can trace any complaint to the right factory.

Then compare return reasons by supplier every few months.

(Disclosure: I work on the sourcing team at LYBAM GLOBAL in Shenzhen.)

I think there are a lot of factors that affect this decision. For very low volumes, it makes sense to just stick to one supplier. For higher volumes over 2k+ a month, maybe you can look to diversify, but I would not recommend doing that for your flagship products; maybe start with products not being sold much. Also, one more thing to consider here is how much margin you are increasing… after deducting the shipping costs, if there isn’t a very consequential difference in your profits, then it’s not worth the headache. Also, to answer your last question, usually people who have diversified suppliers are people with high volumes who naturally have resources or staff to handle it.

ai_summary.summarized_text:
The discussion focuses on when a seller should move beyond a single supplier, particularly after tariff-related disruptions raised concerns that delays can leave every sales channel out of stock. No universal revenue or volume threshold emerged; participants generally framed diversification around the risk of a supplier becoming a single point of failure, weighed against the added costs and workload.

Suggested warning signs include shipment delays that would cause prolonged stockouts, drifting lead times, inconsistent paperwork or payments, and no viable backup for the same product specifications. One participant suggested that more than 30 days of potential stockout exposure signals high risk and proposed keeping a backup active with some orders; another recommended testing that supplier with a small order first. A separate view suggested considering diversification above roughly 2,000 units per month, while cautioning against starting with flagship products and urging sellers to assess the impact on margins.

To maintain consistent quality, contributors recommended using shared specifications and golden samples, supplier-specific test reports, identical inspection checklists, batch tracking, and periodic comparison of returns. The discussion remains open, with no agreed threshold or decision rule.
